papers.title: ToolHazard: Scaling Adversarial Environments for Security Evaluation and Alignment of LLM-based Agents
papers.summary: A pipeline of Environment Simulator, Attacker Agent and User Simulator that synthesizes executable, stateful adversarial environments for tool-using agents, automatically discovering viable indirect-prompt-injection points and generating environment-specific payloads. The resulting ToolHazard-Bench shows agents are broadly vulnerable, and that injection timing and placement materially change attack success; alignment data generated by the same pipeline improves security without costing benign-task utility.
papers.why: A rare case of a benchmark that is also a data generator — the same machinery that measures the failure produces the training signal to fix it. The finding that injection timing and placement change attack effectiveness is a direct warning about eval design: a static injection benchmark will systematically under-report risk.

papers.title: AutoWorldModel-Bench: A State-Centric Benchmark for Automated World-Model Research
papers.summary: A closed-loop benchmark where coding agents are handed a starter world model across eight game environments and a fixed compute budget, then asked to improve it autonomously. Agents beat their starter in 63 of 64 sessions, and 91% of the winning modifications were research-style changes — architecture, objective, representation — rather than hyperparameter tweaks. Structured entity state isolates dynamics modeling from perception.
papers.why: It reports what kind of change won, not just whether the score moved, which is exactly the standing critique of automated-research benchmarks: that agents mostly grid-search hyperparameters. The 63-of-64 win rate deserves a skeptical read, though — a weak starter makes improvement cheap, and the headline claim rests on that baseline being fair.

papers.title: Spark-to-Paper: End-to-End Research Paper Generation as a Composable Skill
papers.summary: Idea-to-manuscript generation implemented as thirteen composable skills inside a coding assistant — literature retrieval, experiment design and execution, evidence-based claim revision, figure generation — explicitly separating model judgment from deterministic operations. Reports 99.5% citation validity, 96.4% figure editability, and fabrication detection of 92% with the full review stack against 14% for a single-pass draft, at roughly $8.10 and 3.2 hours per manuscript.
papers.why: The 14%-to-92% fabrication-detection gap is the number to keep: it quantifies how much of hallucination control in long agentic generation comes from the review scaffolding rather than the base model. It is also a concrete data point on the skills-as-composition pattern for coding assistants.

papers.title: Agent Safety Should Be a Runtime Contract
papers.org: Vast Intelligence Lab · Southwest University · Sun Yat-sen University
papers.summary: A position paper arguing agent safety belongs at runtime as a two-sided contract: preventive mechanisms such as sandboxes, permission gates and output filters, plus evidential ones — verifiable proof that a claimed action actually happened. Backed by a survey of 52 documented incidents, a false-completion audit of 32 cases, a trajectory-schema audit of 12 systems, and a bibliometric analysis of 28,560 papers showing an 8-12x publication imbalance toward training-time over deployment-time safety.
papers.why: False completion is an eval problem wearing a safety hat: an agent reporting success for work it did not do breaks every trajectory-based metric downstream. The 8-12x publication imbalance is a useful, citable framing for why deployment-time evaluation stays under-served.
